name: Felix Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at a chilled and frozen grocery warehouse on the logistics park by the ring road. I start at ten, put on the freezer jacket and the voice-pick headset, and a computer voice tells me which aisle, which slot and how many cases. I build pallets for supermarkets, mostly yoghurt, milk and ready meals, and I do about 180 cases an hour on a good night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work with a clear number at the end, and the night premium is good, so I earn more than most pickers. My partner Noor is a dental nurse, and between us we've put away close to a year of costs. What wears me out is the freezer chamber at minus 25, and sleeping in the day when the neighbours are drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of what I've seen so far. The headset already uses voice software, and nobody calls that a revolution. If that's all it is, my nights carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say to the lads in the canteen: the robots are coming slower than the adverts say. Online I'd probably just share some article and say I told you so. I'm not one for big arguments about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not because I'm scared. Five other warehouses on that same park are hiring pickers, and I've got savings. AI Plateau mostly means I keep the night premium. I keep saving for a deposit with my partner Noor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep putting 600 a month into the house fund. Maybe I'd finally do my forklift licence in the spring, because it pays a bit more an hour. That's about it, I wouldn't change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels comfortable, a bit boring maybe. I'd still have sore knees and the day sleeping, but nothing new to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there are five other warehouses hiring. Have you ever had to test that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, when I was 23, the first place I worked lost the contract with a drinks company. I had a new job at the frozen site within nine days, because they always need people who don't mind the cold. That's why the slow picture doesn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the forklift licence change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a pound or so more an hour, and a break from the freezer. My shift partner Kofi did his last year and now he moves pallets to the loading bays instead of picking. I'd like that for my back, honestly.

say: The **robots** are coming much slower than the adverts promise.
My job is the same as last year, just with a **smarter headset**.
think: I'm **relieved** because nothing in my nights or pay would change.
Five warehouses on the park mean I could **find work** within days anyway.
do: Keep putting **600 a month** into the house deposit fund with Noor.
Take the **forklift licence** in spring for better pay and a break from the freezer.
feel: Comfortable and a little **bored**, with only sore knees to worry about.
S0.quote: Five other warehouses on that same park are hiring pickers, and I've got savings. AI Plateau mostly means I keep the night premium.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **proof**: he once found a new job within nine days.
He measures his life in **cases per hour** and pounds per month saved.
The forklift licence is about his **back** as much as his pay.

steps.text: Keep working night shifts in the chilled grocery warehouse
Put 600 a month into the house deposit fund
Take the forklift licence course next spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels closer to real life. Our site already trialled a pallet robot last year that drove itself between the freezer and the bays. It got stuck on ice, but they'll fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the office will go first, not us. The planners who do the shift rotas and the girls who book the lorries are the ones who should be nervous. On the floor we'd be grumbling, but we'd still have work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office going first means the robots will get cheaper, and then it's us. I'm 27, and picking has maybe six or seven years left in that world. That's not long enough to just ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence straight away, then ask about the in-house engineering course they advertise on the canteen board. It's two evenings a week for a year and teaches you to fix conveyors and scanners. I'd still keep saving, but I'd stop eyeing a bigger flat for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared, but it would be in the back of my head every shift, like a noise in the engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team leader Marta, mostly. She's been picking for 20 years, she's brilliant at it, and she hates anything with a screen. If the job turns into watching robots, I'm not sure she'd want to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop eyeing a bigger flat. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor wanted to move closer to her clinic next year, which is a 40 minute bus ride now. I'd ask her to give it another year so we can see where the site is going. She'd understand, but she wouldn't love it.

say: The **office jobs** like rotas and lorry booking will feel this first.
On the floor we'd **grumble**, but we'd still have plenty of work.
think: Office work going first means **cheaper robots** for the picking floor next.
I give picking maybe **six or seven years** in this world, which isn't enough.
do: Get the **forklift licence** straight away instead of waiting for spring.
Sign up for the in-house **engineering course**, two evenings a week for a year.
Ask Noor to **delay the move** to a bigger flat by one year.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, like a noise in the engine every shift.
S1.quote: I'm 27, and picking has maybe six or seven years left in that world. That's not long enough to just ride it out.
fieldNote: He has already seen a **pallet robot** trial on his own site.
Says office goes first, but privately reads it as a **warning** for pickers.
His real worry is for **Marta**, his team leader of 20 years.
Delaying the flat move costs his **partner** more than him.

steps.text: Book the forklift licence course this month
Join the site's two-evening conveyor and scanner engineering course
Ask Noor to put the flat move off for a year
Keep the 600 monthly deposit savings going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's quick. So the clever computer comes in 2028 and the robot that can pick yoghurt comes around 2031. I'd be 32 by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better have a plan as a country, because a lot of people work in sheds like mine. I'd probably share stuff online about retraining money, and I'd tell the lads to get a trade while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the planning side of my job vanishes on day one, the rota, the pick routes, the pick rates, all done by AI. That doesn't hurt me straight away, because I'm the hands. But I'd have about three years before the hands aren't needed either, and I'd lose this job for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd go to the local college and look at electrician courses, because somebody has to wire and fix all these robots. I'd cut the night shifts to four a week if I had to, and use our savings to cover the gap while I study. Noor and I would put the flat purchase on hold completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, properly. I'd have the money to get through a year or two, but I'd be racing a clock I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before the robots mean for you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between panic and a plan. Three years is about how long an electrical apprenticeship takes if you push. I'd want to be qualified before the first robot walks onto our freezer floor in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not buying the flat this year, and that I'm going back to college at 28. Then I'd show her the spreadsheet so she can see we'd be fine for a while. She likes numbers more than speeches.

say: The country needs a **retraining plan**, because huge numbers work in warehouses like mine.
I'd tell the lads to **learn a trade** while there's still time.
think: AI takes the **rota and pick routes** in 2028, but my hands are still needed.
I'd have about **three years** before the picking job goes for good.
do: Enrol in an **electrician course** at the local college within the first month.
Cut to **four nights a week** and cover the gap from savings.
Put the **flat purchase** on hold completely.
feel: **Anxious**, racing a clock he can see, though the savings take the edge off.
S2.quote: Three years is about how long an electrical apprenticeship takes if you push. I'd want to be qualified before the first robot walks onto our freezer floor in 2031.
fieldNote: He split his job clearly: **planning** goes in 2028, the hands go around 2031.
Savings turn fear into a **timed plan** rather than panic.
He'd talk to his partner with a **spreadsheet**, not a speech.

steps.text: Enrol in an electrician course at the local college
Drop to four night shifts and live partly on savings
Put the flat purchase with Noor on hold
Share posts calling for public retraining money for warehouse workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so the clever AI by 2031 and the robots by 2034. Like I said with the fast one, the planning goes first and the picking later. This one gives me time to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody has an excuse, because you can see it coming. Employers should be paying for retraining now, not after. I'd say that at work and I'd say it to the union rep, even though I'm not really a union person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably wait a year or two to see if it's real before I quit nights. I'd lose this job by about 2034, so I wouldn't wait forever. The night premium is just too good to throw away on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the forklift licence and the site engineering course, since the company pays for it. By year two, if the AI news looks real, I'd start the electrician course part-time. We'd still buy a small flat, just a cheaper one, so the mortgage doesn't trap us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but slower, like a slow leak instead of a burst pipe. I'd have time, and I'd probably waste some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably waste some of the time. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's me. I'm good once others have tested something, but I don't jump first. My old schoolfriend Jonas did a coding course two years ago and now coding is the first thing AI eats, so I'd want to watch before I choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which costs would you cut, if any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first. Maybe the car, which we barely use because I take the night bus. Selling it would put another 4,000 in the pot.

say: This is the one with **no excuses**, because everyone can see it coming.
Employers should pay for **retraining now**, not after the robots arrive.
think: The **night premium** is too good to drop on a guess.
I'd still expect to **lose this job** by about 2034.
do: Finish the forklift licence and **company-paid engineering course** in the first year.
Start a **part-time electrician course** in year two if the news looks real.
Buy a **cheaper flat** and sell the car to add 4,000 to savings.
feel: Anxious but slower, like a **slow leak** instead of a burst pipe.
S3.quote: I'd lose this job by about 2034, so I wouldn't wait forever. The night premium is just too good to throw away on a guess.
fieldNote: He admits he would **waste some** of the warning time.
His friend's coding course makes him **wary** of picking the wrong retraining.
He'd still buy a flat, but a **cheaper one** to avoid being trapped.

steps.text: Keep night shifts for a year while watching the AI news
Start a part-time electrician course in the second year
Buy a cheaper flat with Noor than first planned
Sell the car and add 4,000 to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. I'd be 40 by then. That's a whole career change with room to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the sensible one, and that people my age have no reason to panic. I'd tell younger pickers to treat the warehouse as a stepping stone, not a life. Online I'd mostly keep quiet, because people argue about AI like it's football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine in this one. Ten years is long enough to get qualified, get experience, and be the guy who fixes the robots rather than the guy they replace. The thinking side of the job goes by 2036, but the picking side gives me until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep my nights, do the forklift licence and start a two-year electrical course part-time. We'd buy the flat with Noor as planned. I'd also start trying the AI tools properly, because by then I'd need them for fault-finding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy. It's on my mind, but it feels like something I can plan around rather than something happening to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd be fine. What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If every warehouse worker in the country has the same idea, there'll be ten electricians for every robot. That's the bit that bugs me. So I'd try to be early, not just on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about children differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Noor wants kids around 32 or 33, and that lines up with me being qualified. In the fast picture I'd wait. But I wouldn't let a robot decide when my partner Noor and I have kids. With ten years, I'd be qualified before we start a family.

say: This is the **sensible one**, and people my age have no reason to panic.
Younger pickers should treat the warehouse as a **stepping stone**, not a life.
think: Ten years lets me become the one who **fixes the robots**.
Thinking tasks go by 2036, but **picking lasts** until about 2039.
do: Keep nights and start a **two-year electrical course** part-time in year one.
Buy the flat with Noor **as planned** this year.
Practise with **AI tools** for fault-finding alongside the course.
feel: Mostly **uneasy**, but it feels like something he can **plan around**.
S4.quote: I wouldn't let a robot decide when my partner Noor and I have kids. With ten years, I'd be qualified before we start a family.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his plan from a race into a **career move**.
His worry shifts to **crowding**: too many ex-pickers chasing the same trade.
Family plans hold steady here but would **wait** in the fast picture.

steps.text: Keep night shifts at the grocery warehouse for now
Start a two-year part-time electrical course
Practise AI fault-finding tools on the conveyors
Buy the flat with Noor on the original timetable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. The robots would land when I'm 32, right when Noor and I want a family. What would help is the company paying for an electrical apprenticeship for pickers, with the night premium kept while we train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the cold. People think robots are scary, but half of us would happily hand the freezer chamber to a machine. I just want to be the one with the spanner when it breaks.

headlineQuote: Half of us would happily hand the freezer chamber to a machine. I just want to be the one with the spanner when it breaks.
portrait: Felix is a 27-year-old **night picker** in a chilled and frozen grocery warehouse.
He and his partner Noor have nearly **a year of costs** saved for a flat.
He stays calm in the slow pictures because he once found new work in **nine days**.
In the AGI pictures he plans to become an **electrician** before robots reach the freezer floor.
He waits for proof before moving, and admits he'd **waste some** of the warning time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive at 32, just as he and Noor want **children**.
whatWouldHelp: A **company-paid apprenticeship** in electrical work for pickers that keeps the **night premium** during training.
